utterances.text: And did interrogation of you start there and continue when you were taken to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And at Manjaca, were you also beaten there?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was that on one occasion or more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: On more than one occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did those beatings take place during interrogation, before interrogation, or after interrogation?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Usually when the policemen entered the barns where we were kept they started beating people then, and I was one of those who were beaten.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think it's right that you made two statements whilst you were in custody, detained. When you made those statements, in what sort of condition were you?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I was in a very bad condition as regards my health. I had been beaten up, wounded in the leg, and so on and so forth. So I was not in a very good state.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to ask you a couple more questions about conditions in Manjaca. What sort of food did you get before the arrival of the Red Cross in July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: In the morning we received tea without any sugar, and then in the afternoon we received some sort of soup, but it was more warm water than anything else, and a small slice of bread because a loaf of bread had to be divided among -- among 30 people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you able to say as a result of the -- the food and the treatment how your weight altered?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: During a period of slightly over a month, I lost over 20 kilos.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We've heard evidence that people were sent to do labour - there are documents about that - including the rebuilding, apparently, of a Serb Orthodox Church. Did you take part in any of that labour?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I didn't take part in that. I was not taken there. But I know that others had to work in the woods and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was -- how was -- how were people taken to do the labour? Was it voluntary or were people simply told that they had to do it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: In the camp we had to obey orders. People were taken away in columns guarded by armed people, and that's how they returned them as well. So it was all forcible labour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, in connection with Manjaca can I ask you to look at one last document, please, which is behind your divider 37, and it's 2857. This document which is a list of enemy soldiers taken into custody in Sanica, and it relates to somebody called Esad -- [French on English channel]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's for His Honour Judge Delvoie.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. -- did you know Esad Sinanovic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I didn't know Esad, but I knew a lot of people from Sanski Most who were in Manjaca camp. They were kept in a separate barn.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The -- however, this prisoner was handed over by Inspector Gajic of Kljuc. Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What happened to -- sorry. Was he one of the people who interviewed you?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What happened to Inspector Gajic at the end?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I heard that he either died or committed suicide, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you -- do you recognise the signature of Vinko Kondic on this document?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that it was Vinko's signature. It was probably signed by somebody else in its stead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, may that be marked and admitted, please, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P959, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, I know that has been truncated, this question and answer session, but can I ask you finally this: What effect did your six months or so that you spent in Manjaca have on you?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Terrible consequences. My health is impaired. I'm no longer capable to work or to lead a normal life, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's all I ask you, Mr. Egrlic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I now tender into evidence, please, his 92 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P960, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we would take the usual break now, after which counsel for whichever side they agree to go first will be invited to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, before Mr. Pantelic starts, if I could just remind him, and if he's kind enough and Your Honours, I would like just like a few minutes at the end to raise the administrative matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, sir. You may be seated. Can you hear me? Oh, he is seated. Oh. We thought he was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sitting down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Egrlic. I represent Mr. Zupljanin, and my name is Counsel Pantelic. Tell me, please - I don't think I have found it anywhere in your statements - where did you serve in the army, in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the name of the place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Karlovac, I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you attend the school for reserve officers there?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And after the compulsory military service, did you ever -- were you ever called for training and military manoeuvres in Kljuc municipality?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Which means that you're familiar with the principles of the functioning of the military and the hierarchy, the positions of chain in variable terms?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, you said earlier today when Ms. Korner was questioning you on page 48, lines 20 to 23, that as far as I could understand you, that you been beaten by some reserve policemen in front of the hospital building. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: In front of the SJB and in front of the hospital as well. In two different locations, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You also said that those people who had beaten you were reserve policemen whom you knew, at least some of them, because you went to school with them. Am I interpreting your answer well?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask you, since we are speaking the same language and we've had difficulties with the satellite communication, when I finish my question, could you please pause for anything between three to five seconds for the interpreters to interpret my question and for the typist to be able to record it. Thank you for your understanding. Tell me, please, could you give me the name of some of your colleagues from school who went on to becoming reserve policemen who beat you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: One of them was Boro Ceko.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: From [realtime transcript read in error "Mr."] Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And were there any others?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: The others I knew only by sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you have any of the names?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I don't have any names. I just knew them by sight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: In terms of the transcript at line 2 at page 54, counsel's question, as I recall was, From Kljuc? It is recorded as being "Mr. Kljuc."

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Egrlic, thus you can't remember anybody else, none of those who ill-treated you, as you say, at the time. And that person Ceko, what kind of uniform did he wear? Did he wear an olive-drab uniform? Was he a member of a military unit? Would you allow for that possibility?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: No. He wore a reserve police uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. We'll check that. Mr. Egrlic, on page 38 of today's LiveNote, line 10, there was a reference to a curfew being introduced. You are an educated person and you also had some military knowledge at the time. You will agree with me that when a curfew is introduced under certain circumstances that that is a legitimate measure? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Under the circumstances as they were in Kljuc, there was no need for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, let's rewind a bit. My question was this: Under extraordinary circumstances and when some combat operations are underway, would you say that introducing a curfew is a legitimate measure? Yes or no? Listen to my question carefully.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: On page 35, line 8, earlier today, you mentioned that you had attended a meeting in Mr. Zupljanin's office and that on that occasion you were provided an explanation as to why the markings and insignia had been introduced. Do you remember when you said that in response to my learned friend Mrs. Korner's questions?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that on that occasion Mr. Zupljanin mentioned the fact that the family name of his father-in-law was Filipovic and that he had turned to the late Omer with regard to that because they may have been related given the fact that they bore the same family name? Do you remember that detail?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: It is possible, but I really don't remember that particular detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, do you remember that Mr. Zupljanin said that the Law on Internal Affairs had been adopted by Republika Srpska and that that law prescribed certain forms including symbols on military caps or hats and that under that law or pursuant to that law new military -- new police insignia were being introduced? Do you remember that detail?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When did you first hear about the establishment of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Sometime in the second half of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You are an experienced politician and an intellectual, well-educated person. You remember significant events that happened at the time, those that could be put in the context of this case. You remember the developments in the Assembly, the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Do you remember all those developments?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I remember some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you often travel to Sarajevo in order to receive instructions from the headquarters of your party the SDA in the autumn of 1991?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I travelled to Sarajevo on business as the President of the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly. I don't know how often I went to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well -- very well. It's all justified and legitimate. You met with the political leaders of the SDA, of course, and you had political consultations with them and that was all part of your duty. Wouldn't that be correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You remember the events in the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina when a vote was taken on the declaration on the independence and sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina. SDA and HDZ MPs over-voted SDS MPs who walked out in protest. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And what happened then were the developments that led to the establishment of Republika Srpska, and that was on the 9th of January, 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, it seems that I have come across in one of your statements a reference to the time when you drafted joint announcements with the MBO party, and you mentioned certain vital interests of the Muslim people or, rather, the population in Kljuc. Am I right? I believe that I have paraphrased your sentence quite well. Just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: It's possible. I really don't know what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let me jog your memory. I'm talking about the joint activities of the SDA and the MBO in Kljuc on the occasion of the initiative and voting of the SDS in Kljuc municipality about ratifying the decision on joining the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Do you remember those political developments at the local level? Do you or do you not?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And then your position was that that was contrary to the vital interests of the Muslim people in Kljuc. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That element, namely the vital interest of every people in Bosnia is very important. We're talking about the foundations of Bosnia and Herzegovina even as we know it today. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So there should be no over-voting when it comes to the vital interests of any of the peoples.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And every people has its representatives in certain bodies and should have the right of veto to block a decision directed against a vital interest of any of the peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croats, Bosniaks, and Serbs alike. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And naturally that principle is in power as well today. It's all very clearly defined in the Dayton Accords; right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When you visited Sarajevo in 1991, and I believe in early 1992 as well, did you at the meetings among the leadership of your party discuss international initiatives, such, for example, those directed at finding a peaceful settlement to the conflict in Bosnia and political problems? Remember, there were a lot of activities within the international community at the time.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: There were, yes, but I didn't take part in such meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, as an intelligent and educated man and as a leader of the party in Kljuc, you probably followed the press and the media. You remember that at the time there was some discussion of cantonisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, of establishing certain regions and districts. Remember such ideas? It was in early 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And it seems to me that you were either a minister or some other high official after the war in the Sana Una Canton; right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Probably a minister of civil engineering.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Of industry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Are you still a member of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: At the local level, or are you a member of the Main Board at the level of the Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And the Sana Una Canton is part of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina; right? The Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina has eight or nine cantons, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Ten.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, we didn't get an answer to the question whether he was a member of the Main Board. They didn't hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, would you please repeat your answer when I asked you whether you were a member of the Main Board at the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina of the SDA. Please tell me what was your answer.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I'm not. I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Therefore, we agreed that there had been certain efforts within the international community to reach a peaceful settlement. We agreed that the principles of cantonisation were discussed. We agreed that Republika Srpska had been set up and that the federation was set up between the Croats and Muslims in Bosnia and that all of that put together comprises the nowadays independent and sovereign unified Bosnia and Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: For the sake of the transcript, you're not a constitutional law expert, are you?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Similarly, you're not an expert for international public law and similar matters?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Why did you, then, in replying to the Prosecutor use the formulation that Republika Srpska and that organisation was a para-state? How do you find yourself to be entitled to call something a para-state when you don't know what the elements of statehood are? Why did you state that that was a para-state? Do you have something against Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: At the time, it was a para-state.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So it is simply an emotional attitude of yours. You're not really qualified to assess whether something is a para-state. Is that right, Mr. Egrlic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Well, I know what elements a state needs to have, what organs, and my personal feelings are on top of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. Now that you've broached this subject, please tell me, what does a state need to have in order to be called a state? Give me the elements, please, or maybe I should assist you. Would you like me to? It would be faster. Does it need to have a central government?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Does it need to have territory?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Does the central government need to control the territory?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, then, in 1992 did the central government in Sarajevo control the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: It didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. That was sufficient with regard to these constitutional topics. We can move on now. Mr. Egrlic, please tell me, when an order from the TO staff of Bosnia-Herzegovina arrived -- and I think that its commander was a certain Colonel Efendic; right? I apologise. My colleague is indicating that I need to correct it. The TO commander in 1992 was Colonel Hasan Efendic; right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And since the JNA had fallen apart, each ethnic group in Bosnia and Herzegovina started establishing its own armed forces; rights?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The Croats had the Croatian Defence Council, abbreviated HVO.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And as one of their symbols on their uniforms was a chequer-board; right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: As for the TO at the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it was actually a precursor to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Various generals and leaders at the time called it the Patriotic League and similar names. We don't need to repeat that, but you know what I'm aiming at; right? And the symbol of that armed formation were the lilies; right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: That was in the course of 1993, and I testified about 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, I'm just wondering where we're going with all of this in relation to the evidence offered by this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one more question to round off the topic of insignia and put an end to that topic. We lose a lot of time on that topic. The Prosecutor keeps bringing up the insignia, and we can agree that each side had their own insignia and it was all legitimate, and I don't see why that needs to be repeated with every witness. Just one more question, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So let us move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, in 1992, in the then Bosnia-Herzegovina, all three sides had their own individual insignia. The Serbs had a tricolour flag like the one we saw on the police cap. The Muslim forces had lilies, and the Croats had a chequer-board symbol. You agree? And then we can move on.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: That was towards the end of 1992 and early 1993. Initially there was the coat of arms of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that had been defined by the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Today in your examination-in-chief you discussed the phenomenon known as Sehid. Over the break we looked up what encyclopedias have and saw that there was this formulation. The combatants who were killed during the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina are known as Sehids if they were members of the Bosnian Muslim Corps. This strictly refers to soldiers, but are you familiar with this formulation, and do you know that it is being used in Bosnia and Herzegovina to this day?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Depends on who's using it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, it is used when referring to soldiers who were killed.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Today, on page 22; when you spoke of the Laniste 2 grave, were soldiers from the Muslim units from the territory of Kljuc also buried in that grave?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: No, there are just civilians there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And where are the soldiers from the Kljuc unit buried?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: None of them were killed. They were taken out of their houses and shot to death as civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So you're telling us now -- actually, let's first clarify this. You arrived in Manjaca towards late May of 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: In early June.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Were there any victims on the Muslim TO side in Kljuc up until that moment? Do you know of anybody who was killed?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, nobody was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And later on when your compatriots came up there and when you met them at Manjaca and later on, after 1992 as well, none of the members of the Muslim TO in Kljuc were killed. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Nobody was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Nobody was killed. Two armies were fighting, two armed formations were fighting and nobody killed on the Muslim side -- nobody was killed on the Muslim side in Kljuc throughout the war. Is that what you're trying to tell us?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Well, that really wasn't a war. You have a different perception of it. It was just one incident, and that's all there was to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let us look into this. Were there any combat operations in the territory of Kljuc when the 6th Krajina Brigade arrived from Sanski Most? Were there any combat operations at the time?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This is quite new to us. It's really surprising. Were you going to say anything?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I wanted to say that what I just told you is exactly what it is. That's how it always was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Would you please look into the binder, Mr. Egrlic, tab 23. 65 ter 2029. Let me just tell you something, Mr. Egrlic. All these documents came from the Prosecution. We put them in order, and many of them had been used in other cases, in Brdjanin, Krajisnik, where you also testified. There is a number in the upper right corner. That's the number that I was referring to. Mr. Egrlic, please look at page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please put the second page on the screen, please. That's at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You can read it, and you can just confirm for me whether this is correct in order to speed things up. So you spoke about what you knew, saying that a large number of civilians were killed at the school in Velagici; right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And that took place on the 1st of June, 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And what we see here, what you've just read, is the description of that event. It is described how this event was qualified as a war crime against civilian population, and if you turn to page 3, Mr. Egrlic, you can see that; right? Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. On page 3 we see that it was signed by Zoran Babic, Deputy Military Prosecutor; right? And this military prosecutor recommends certain measures in accordance with the law, who needs to be interviewed and various forensic details. We don't need to go into that, but please look at page 1 where there is a request to commence investigation. This is something that the military prosecutor is sending to the military court in Banja Luka; right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And now look under number 5, Mr. Egrlic. First let me ask you, Donje Ratkovo, is that in the Kljuc sector? Under 5.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you know this person Bajic by any chance?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I don't know him. I only heard of him. The name rings a bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And under number 6 I see that that person is from Vrbljane in Kljuc municipality, and the person's name is Cuk, Nikola Cuk. Do you happen to know him? Did you ever hear of him?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Turn to page 2, please. Do you see under name Osan [phoen], a certain Zoran Banjac from the village of Sanica? Did you perhaps know him, or does the name ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I didn't know him, but I am familiar with the family name Banjac in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And what about Milenko Miljevic from Gornji Budelj, did you ever hear of him?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And now -- I have to wait. I'm looking at the transcript. Now it's okay. Let's go on. Under number 10, 11 and 12, you see some names. Do you perhaps know any of them? Does any of the names ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: No, no. No. I don't know them. They don't sound familiar at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would be grateful if this document can be admitted and marked if there is no objection from Prosecution or --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only question I have is do I understand from this line of examination or cross-examination, rather, that Zupljanin is in fact challenging the adjudicated facts which have been admitted in this case not against him? The answer to that is yes, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: For the record, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no objection to being admitted, but it's -- it's a matter, obviously, that we'll now have to take into consideration, because the adjudicated facts are very different from what's in here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 2D42, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now from your previous testimonies in the Brdjanin and Krajisnik cases -- no, no, no, no. Strike that. Let me start with an introduction. Pursuant to an order issued by the BiH TO, the late Omer Filipovic was appointed the commander of the TO unit. He was a reserve officer, and that was the main reason why he had been put up by the TO staff to be a commander. Is that right? Could you please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You were in charge of political issues in the same staff; right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And Captain Amir Abdic was some sort of a military coordinator in charge of matters in the field given his previous experience in the JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Where was Golaja? Where is Golaja? Could you please try and locate that area for us, Golaja.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: That is a part of Sanski Most municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: There was a significant military unit there under the command of Captain Avdic; right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm sure that you also heard that some Serb soldiers had been arrested, and Colonel Basara then negotiated, and finally Serb soldiers were liberated, and Captain Abdic and his troops were seen off to the territory under the control of the BiH Army somewhere in the Bihac area; right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The TO staff which was organised there as the precursor of the ABiH had, according to some assessments and estimates, approximately 1.500 to 2.000 members; right? I'm talking about conscripts.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Taking into account all military conscripts that could have been its potential strength.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Of course, of course. The mobilisation process was underway. We will agree on that; right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, you claim in your statements that the Kljuc TO unit was exclusively established to engage in defence activities; right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I'm not claiming that. It was the period of its infancy and that was its aim.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But it was not envisaged to engage in any offensive operations against the Serbs. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, let's help the Trial Chamber and look at some events together, some of which you're personally familiar with or you heard about them from your fellow citizens or based on some documents. I'm putting it to you that on the 27th of May, 1992, an ambush was set up in the Gornji Ramici sector. You've already testified about that. On that occasion, the assistant commander of the Kljuc SJB, Dusan Stojakovic, was killed, and he was a Serb; right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I don't know all the details, but I know that he was indeed killed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the end of his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the witness said he was known as Duca.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We believe that there was an ambush and that he was killed in that ambush. That's my question.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: We do not agree about the ambush. We are talking about a -- village guards, people who were guarding their own homes. They didn't go to the Serb territory in order to attack anybody there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I don't know [as interpreted] that several people were wounded. One of them was a member of the military police, Zeljko Tesmon [phoen] and a policeman Milos Kecman. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: He was shot at by the Muslim TO; right? They were shot at by the Muslim TO. It's a simple question. Just say yes, no, move on. They were shot at by the Muslim TO.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I suppose so. I don't know who shot at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, never mind, let's move on. Let's go on. And after that does Aziz Gromljic [phoen] ring a well?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, he does.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: He was a retired police officer or a policeman of the federal SUP; right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: He was a member of a special detachment in the federal SUP, but you don't know that, do you?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on. On the 27th May, ambushes were set up in the Busija-Pudin Han sectors. You've already spoken about that. A military column was attacked, the one moving from Knin towards Banja Luka, a military column, a column of the Serb army; right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I've heard of the incidents, but I don't know how things transpired.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you know that two soldiers were killed on that occasion, that six were seriously wounded, and that 27 were slightly wounded, and that four more soldiers subsequently succumbed to their wounds. Do you know of that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And also on the 27th of May in the Tocionik sector -- or, rather, Tocina, I apologise, which is close to the crossroads of roads leading to Kljuc and Sanski Most, another ambush was set up and -- but it was not completed because it was going to be -- to serve an attack on the police detachment. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: On the 27th May, on the same day, the M5 road above the village of Velagici was blown up in order to prevent the transfer of Serbian Army units to various other positions. That operation was carried out using 80 kilogrammes of explosives. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: On that same day, 27 May, again do you know that seven soldiers from a unit in Dobrinja who were out reconnoitering were arrested in the Crljeni sector. Did you hear of that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I heard that that happened on the 26th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: According to our information and based on documents that we received from a very honest officer, Colonel Basara, who placed all of them under his control. We have information that on the 27th of May was the beginning of all the armed conflicts involving the Muslim TO and the military forces of the Serbs. Can we agree on that? Can we agree that that day was when the conflicts really started? Right? Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let me put it to you this way: I didn't want to go into all the details with you because we're short on time, but you say -- you will find that in our binder under tab 21. Could you please look at that. I'm going to tell you that you already spoke about that in the Krajisnik case, if I'm not mistaken. This is a Prosecutor's document which was tendered into evidence. This is a report by the Kljuc SJB which speaks about all those various events, and you spoke at great length about all of them in the other cases, so I don't want to belabour the matter with you, but please look at page 9, Mr. Egrlic. Actually, pages 9, 10, and 11. You will find a lot more details in the descriptions of the events that we have just mentioned. Could you please just confirm for us. Look at pages 9, bullet point 1, and so on and so forth. This is what you will find here.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I have a document, a five-page long document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you look at page 1. What does it say?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Information about a larger number of refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. Sorry. Wrong document. There must have been some confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher -- or the Court Officer, rather, provide the witness with number 21, which is the document in our binder under tab 21 -- or, rather, bearing number 21. I'm sorry, sorry. No, no, no. I apologise. It's a P document. I apologise. It's a P document. Here it is. Sorry. Under number 20. It's a 92 ter binder, a Prosecution document. The Prosecutor's binder. 65 ter number 845. I apologise. My mistake. It's a P document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you have it, Mr. Egrlic? Is that a document from July 1992, information about the work of the SJB?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You saw it already in some other cases, and now could you please look at page 9. Could you kindly look at page 9 in this document. There you have it. Gornji Ramici. Let's move on to page 10, reference to Busija, and Pudin Han, Tocina, and so on and so forth. Well, you see how things are arranged. And these are the events that we've just discussed; right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And you commented on this document in earlier cases too. Thank you, Mr. Egrlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Significant objection or -- I would like -- it's admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's part of 65 ter -- 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Egrlic. This was already admitted as part of the 92 ter package. Thank you very much for this. Now, when Colonel Basara entered the Kljuc area with the 6th Brigade, he, together with Colonel Galic from the Kljuc brigade, the two of them as military officials, as a military unit, place everything under their control, and all of the procedures from that time on had to be authorised in a certain way by military organs.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Egrlic, did you hear that in mid-April 1992, and this is something that was confirmed at the Assembly session in May of 1992 in Banja Luka, that they declared an imminent threat of war? Did you hear of this piece of information?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: At page 73, line 11, and your answer is line 18, your answer was, "I don't know," full stop, "probably." Right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Probably, I don't know. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you as an educated person, as somebody who is aware of general principles. You served in the army. You attended military exercises. When there are military operations in the state of imminent threat of war, then under those circumstances the army is given very specific responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Well, the essential question is what was the army doing there?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Certainly. We'll get to that. But now for the time being, Mr. Egrlic, please tell me, when it comes to the role of the army in the state of imminent threat of war, as an educated, wise man, would you agree with me when I say that at that point in time the army takes on the role of somebody who regulates all aspects of life? Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the case of war, when the war is declared, but Republika Srpska commenced the war on their own initiative in order to clear up the territory and to become a mono-ethnic state.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Egrlic, tell me, please, this: The previous document that we discussed, the one with ambushes and actions and the beginning of the conflict on the 27th of May, 1992, you will agree with me, won't you, that those ambushes and those activities were in their nature offensive activities?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: First of all, we can't agree that those were ambushes. People were there standing guard as local village guards in front of their homes. They did not go over to the Serb territory and do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But wait a second. You will agree with me, won't you, that there were some synchronised activities on the 27th of May in several localities in the Kljuc area and that the Muslim TO carried out certain combat operations, actions. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, wait a second. Who had a conflict then with the Army of Republika Srpska and with the brigade of Colonel Basara? Who was waging a war there? Who was putting up resistance? Who participated in that? Please give me an explanation.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Nobody did. On the 27th of May, they entered without having fired a bullet. They entered and they took up all strategically significant locations, and it wasn't until later when Abdic separated himself and moved on to Golaja.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. That's what I'm interested in. Abdic split away from them, he set up his own unit, and the fighting between the Muslim TO and the units of the Army of Republika Srpska commenced; right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, but that was already some time -- I don't know the date, but it wasn't the dates that we discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Egrlic, let us just look at this document. In the meantime as I'm doing this, would you please tell me, how many Serbs are there living in Kljuc municipality now? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, it's an insignificant number; right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: People simply didn't come back. They sold their properties, and that's how it was. They did it -- they did it have their own will. There could have been more of them living there now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So it was their decision. They sold their properties, and they moved to an area where they want to live; right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And in relation to the pre-war time, I suppose that a large number of other Bosniaks came to Kljuc municipality, that they settled there.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: No, not a lot of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, a certain number came. Now, Mr. Egrlic, now please look at tab 13 in our binder. This is a two-page document dated -- just a second, please. There seems to be another confusion here. My mistake. I apologise. Twenty-five. Twenty-five. I'm really sorry. Tab 25. 2D05-0071. My associates sent it today by mail, by e-mail, under number 20 today. Mr. Egrlic, is this document discussion SDA and MBO?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: No. This is the information on the work of a group in Kljuc municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, then something else there. We are changing it now. Would you please see whether it's under tab 25. That's a document we sent today. 2D05-0071. While we are looking for the document, Mr. Egrlic, I will tell you what this is about. That was a debate between the SDA and the MBO, and what they discussed at the time was certain anxiety among the population leaving the ARK Krajina. You participated, and then Mr. Omer Filipovic, and then some other people. Do you remember about this? It was on the 16th of January, 1992, and you testified about this in Krajisnik; right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The point of that release, press release, was that -- do you have the document in front of you? All right. Now all of us have it. Great. So the point of that report -- oh, let me ask you this first: Nihad Filipovic is acting as a greater Catholic than the Pope. So what was that supposed to mean? What was he doing? He was from the Liberal Party. So what was the reason he was described in this way?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Where does it say so?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Towards the end. Two -- ninth line from the bottom. It says "Nihad Filipovic." Have you found it? Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So you knew Nihad Filipovic; right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: He was a leader or something else within that Liberal Party in Kljuc; right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I don't know which party he represented.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What -- what was this supposed to mean in this joint release, that he was a greater Catholic than the Pope? What was his position? What platform did he advocate?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. I need to see what it says here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, but at some point could you take the break until tomorrow morning. You remember Ms. Korner asked for a few minutes to deal with some matters before we take the evening's adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm very mindful about that, Your Honour, and I think that this is a proper moment to take a break. Because in the meantime, I suggest to Mr. Egrlic to take a look at these documents, and then we can go much faster tomorrow. This document and other documents, too, so that we can finish tomorrow. [Interpretation] That won't take a lot of time. Thank you, Mr. Egrlic. See you -- or, rather, talk to you tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, we are about to adjourn for the evening. There are some procedural matters with which the Chamber must deal, but your testimony's not at an end, so you would be excused at this point, but you will resume -- we will resume at 2.15 tomorrow afternoon. That's 2.15 local time in The Hague, whatever the time is in Sarajevo. The -- because you are sworn as a witness, I must remind you that you can't discuss your testimony with anyone. So you are now excused to return tomorrow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, thank you very much. The first administrative matter is this: Because of the gap we've had to reorganise the witnesses. And so Witness 187 for whom a safe conduct was issued between various dates, could we alter the dates, please, from the 6th to the 13th of March. The safe conduct originally was for -- I can't remember what day. I no longer remember the dates, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Are safe conduct orders time limited.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, no, they're time limited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: They expire when the within has given testimony?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think so. I think we gave a range of dates, but I can check -- or maybe Mr. Dygeus can check that. But in any event, it started on the date before he was due to testify which will no longer be the date, so we'd like it altered to the 6th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber will see to it that the necessary writing -- the necessary amendment is done in writing. Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honours, the second matter is this: Tomorrow's witness deals quite extensively in the statement, which is part of the 92 package, with exhumations. This is the second witness who can, if required, deal with exhumations. He was present at a great deal. Now, as yet we haven't really had an indication from the Defence whether exhumation evidence is something that can be agreed, and we keep on -- as I say, the second witness. We're going to have a number of witnesses who could deal with it if it's going to be the subject of dispute. So what we're really asking for is a general indication, no more than that, that the detail can be worked out tomorrow before the witness is called whether or not witnesses who can actually deal with the -- what exhumations were carried out and when and the documentation will be required to give evidence about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So counsel would consult, and they will let you know what the position is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly. I've mentioned this to both sets of counsel, but obviously it's preferable if they could at least just turn their mind perhaps into overnight and tomorrow morning as to whether this evidence is likely to be disputed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So they have been reminded.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could counsel indicate in the presence of the Chamber when the OTP might expect an answer to assist them in how they, therefore, conduct their examination of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we will -- we will do our best, Your Honour, to -- to advise Ms. Korner and the -- the OTP of our position before they start tomorrow with the witness. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: As counsel for the Defence may be aware, there is before the Chamber a sixth application for adjudicated facts, and the -- having regard to the fact that it is well known this is -- this is a ruling on which the Chamber is anxiously working, the expedited response from the Defence on this most resent application would be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. We're aware of that, and we intend to file it by end of this week. Thank you.
